edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on all six pages. The id is missing; only a bare page number is printed at the right.

edits.quote: In every problem, blocks must stay inside the shape and must not overlap.
edits.fix: Add 'and follow the lines', as the 2–3 rule does. K–1 children will otherwise set blocks across grid lines. That changes the Problem 6 game, because a straddling block leaves unusable gaps, and it muddles the Problem 5 moves.

edits.quote: Build the left picture with blue blocks, then change it into the right picture in as few moves as you can. A move turns three blue blocks that make a hexagon, like this:
edits.fix: The two-hexagon demonstration (with the double arrow) sits directly above the two task pairs and is itself a 'left picture' and a 'right picture'. Give the move and its demo first, then write 'Build each big picture with blue blocks and change it into the small picture beside it, in as few moves as you can.' Alternatively, set the demo apart (smaller and boxed) so children do not read it as a third task. Checked answers: 2 moves and 4 moves.
Add 'Circle first or second.' to the problem so children know how to record. Checked answers: hexagon, go second (mirror through the centre); both strips, go first (take the middle, then mirror).

k-1.summary: This is a substantial, concrete K–1 sheet with actual-size boards throughout. It runs from possible and impossible blue covers (three of six even-area shapes are impossible) to the fewest green triangles on triangles of side 2–5 with a prediction step, all coverings of two small hexagons (2 and 3), flip puzzles (2 and 4 moves) and a first/second-player game, and every answer checks out. The edits are small clarity fixes: add 'follow the lines' (the game needs it), separate the move demo from the Problem 5 tasks, add 'circle', and fix the footer id.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on all eight pages. The id is missing.

edits.quote: Which of these boards can be covered with blue blocks only?
edits.fix: Delete it. The next two sentences already say to cover each board you can, draw the lines, and put an X on the rest, so the question only repeats the task. Checked: A, C and F can be covered; B (5 up, 3 down), D (6 up, 4 down) and E (7 up, 5 down) cannot.

edits.quote: Each board below is a big hexagon with two gray holes, and no block may cover a hole.
edits.fix: Shorten to 'No block may cover a gray hole.' The diagrams already show the hexagons and holes. Checked: A and D can be covered (4 coverings each); B (two up holes) and C (two down holes) cannot.

grades-2-3.summary: This is the strongest band: a well-sequenced development of the up/down coloring obstruction. It goes from six actual-size boards, through the fewest green triangles (2, 3, 4, 5) and hexagons with holes, to a proof for triangle C, the n-greens generalization (10 and 100), purple versus blue (purple is never better: 4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5) and a design-a-board challenge. All diagrams and claims are correct. It needs only two one-line trims and the footer id.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on all eight pages. The id is missing.

edits.quote: How many different ways can it be covered with blue blocks?
edits.fix: The opening rule already says boards are covered with blue blocks only. Drop the repeated 'with blue blocks' in P8 and P9 (the same phrase appears in 'How many different ways can the big hexagon be covered with blue blocks?').

edits.quote: For the first pair, explain why it cannot be done in fewer moves.
edits.fix: The first pair joins the two extreme coverings and needs 8 moves, the most the flip graph allows. Proving 8 is minimal needs an invariant (cube count, or chains, where each move swaps one adjacent LR pair) that the packet only builds in P5–P7. Move this demand to the end of P7 ('Use this to explain why the first pair in Problem 3 needs 8 moves'), or leave it to the adult. The second pair (4 moves) is correct.

edits.quote: Can this be done in exactly 4 moves? In 5? In 6? In 7? For each number, draw the coverings you pass through, or explain why it cannot be done.
edits.fix: 4 and 6 are possible; 5 and 7 are impossible because the flip graph is bipartite. Children can only justify the impossible cases with the parity fact from P7, so move P4 to after P7 (renumber), where the chain fact settles the odd lengths.

edits.quote: Eight small hexagon copies under Problem 4; the bottom half of the page is blank.
edits.fix: Showing a 4-move and a 6-move round trip takes 10 drawings, and only 8 copies are given. Add a third row of four copies in the blank space.

edits.quote: This board has only one small edge on its bottom side.
edits.fix: Delete it. The diagram shows the edge, and the sentence points children straight at the one-chain method (3 L and 3 R, so 20 ways). Let them see that themselves.

edits.quote: If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back.
edits.fix: There are 16 copies for 20 coverings. Pages are single-sided, so children would have to draw hexagon grids freehand on the back. Add a fifth row of copies in the blank space below the grid and delete the sentence.

grades-4-5.summary: This band covers kernel 2 thoroughly and correctly: the 6 coverings of the 2-1-2 hexagon and their flip graph, flip routes on the big hexagon (8 and 4 moves), round trips (4 and 6 yes, 5 and 7 no), and chains. The example chain is RLLR as stated, and P6 has two possible and two impossible pairs. It ends with counting via chains (20 and 20). The main edits are sequencing, because the P3 and P4 proof demands come before the chain invariant they need, plus recording-copy and small wording fixes.

overall.strongest: Grades 2–3 develops the up/down coloring obstruction through a well-chosen sequence: actual-size possible/impossible boards, fewest-green triangles, holed hexagons, proof and generalization, purple versus blue, and a design problem, all with correct answers and almost no wasted words.
overall.weakest: The 4–5 sequence asks children to prove the 8-move minimum (P3) and the impossibility of odd round trips (P4) before P5–P7 give them the chain invariant those proofs need; the K–1 rule also omits 'follow the lines', which its game depends on.
